entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Penguin Books, founded in 1935 by Allen Lane in London, is the publisher most responsible for democratizing reading in the 20th century: by producing quality paperback books at sixpence — the price of a packet of cigarettes — Penguin made literature accessible to working-class readers who could not afford hardback prices, fundamentally changing who reads and what reading means in modern society. The Penguin brand — with its distinctive banded cover design — became one of the most recognizable in publishing history.

Allen Lane conceived Penguin Books at Exeter station after visiting Agatha Christie and discovering no affordable quality books available for his train journey. He launched Penguin in 1935 with 10 titles, including works by Ernest Hemingway, Agatha Christie, and André Maurois, sold in Woolworth's stores. The sixpenny price — enabling book-buying as a casual purchase rather than major expenditure — democratized reading across Britain's class structure. The paperback revolution Lane launched transformed global publishing.

Penguin's 1960 trial for publishing D.H. Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover — prosecuted under the Obscene Publications Act — and its acquittal by jury on 2 November 1960 was a landmark victory for literary freedom. The prosecuting counsel's famous question 'Is it a book you would wish your wife or servants to read?' demonstrated the prosecution's class assumptions. Two million copies sold in the first week after acquittal. Penguin Classics, Puffin (children's books), and Pelican (non-fiction) extended the Penguin brand across all publishing categories.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Allen Lane's invention of the affordable quality paperback at sixpence — 'the price of a packet of cigarettes' — democratized reading for working-class Britain and launched the paperback revolution that transformed global publishing and literary access.
